claim: Aging is associated with an increased proportion of NMJs that display degenerated pre/post-synaptic morphologies in both tibialis anterior (TA) and diaphragm muscles.
source: Aging is associated with an increased proportion of NMJs that display degenerated pre/post-synaptic morphologies in both tibialis anterior (TA) and diaphragm muscles (Figure 1A–E) (Gonzalez-Freire et al., 2014; Valdez et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-E and citations to previous literature (Gonzalez-Freire et al., 2014; Valdez et al., 2010, 2012).

claim: Very few aged NMJs were completely denervated despite a high proportion of degenerated NMJs.
source: Although we observed a high proportion of degenerated NMJs in aged muscles, very few were completely denervated (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B and D.

claim: Gene sets associated with acetylcholine receptor (AChR) activity and neurotransmission were highly enriched in 6M-Syn samples.
source: As expected, gene sets associated with acetylcholine receptor (AChR) activity and neurotransmission were highly enriched in 6M-Syn samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) (Chakkalakal and Jasmin, 2003; Merlie and Sanes, 1985; Hippenmeyer et al., 2007; Kishi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, and citations to previous literature.

claim: Aged muscles did not show elevation or extra-synaptic induction of synaptic gene expression, consistent with low levels of complete denervation.
source: Although we observed previously described alterations in mitochondrial metabolism and atrophy-related genes in 24M-ExS and 24M-Syn samples, consistent with low levels of complete denervation we did not observe elevation or extra-synaptic induction of synaptic gene expression (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H) (Hippenmeyer et al., 2007; Kishi et al., 2005; Ibebunjo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H, and citations to previous literature.

claim: Comparison of 6M-Syn and 24M-Syn samples revealed age-related declines in synapse-specific gene expression.
source: However, comparison of 6M-Syn and 24M-Syn samples revealed age-related declines in synapse-specific gene expression, indicating a possible loss of post-synaptic myonuclei, the source of synapse-specific mRNAs at NMJs (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H.

claim: The size of NMJs, based on post-synaptic apparatus volume and cumulative AChR intensity, positively correlated with the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters.
source: The size of NMJs, based on post-synaptic apparatus volume and cumulative AChR intensity, positively correlated with the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of degenerated NMJs had few post-synaptic myonuclei.
source: Notably, the majority of degenerated NMJs had few post-synaptic myonuclei (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The fraction of aged NMJ post-synaptic myonuclear clusters with greater than 4 myonuclei was significantly lower compared to adult.
source: We observed that the fraction of aged NMJ post-synaptic myonuclear clusters with greater than 4 myonuclei, in comparison to adult, was significantly lower (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: Loss of post-synaptic myonuclei is a predominant feature of aged degenerated NMJs.
source: Therefore, loss of post-synaptic myonuclei is a predominant feature of aged degenerated NMJs.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing reduced post-synaptic myonuclei in aged NMJs.

claim: SC frequency significantly declined at 18 and 24 months regardless of their source (Syn vs ExS regions).
source: Regardless of their source (Syn vs ExS regions), SC frequency significantly declined at 18 and 24 months (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: At 6 and 12 months, GFP-labeled SC derived contribution was found at myofiber ends and/or middle portions of myofibers where NMJs are located.
source: At 6 and 12 months we found GFP-labeled SC derived contribution at myofiber ends where sarcomere addition can occur (Williams and Goldspink, 1971; Zhang and McLennan, 1995; Wang et al., 2010), and/or middle portions of myofibers where NMJs are located (Liu et al., 2015) (Figure 3A,B and D).
evidence: Supported by single myofiber analysis shown in Figure 3A, B and D, and citations to previous literature.

claim: Six weeks after tamoxifen administration, GFP-labeled post-synaptic myonuclei were observed at NMJs.
source: Consistent with SCs as a cellular source, 6 weeks after tamoxifen administration GFP-labeled post-synaptic myonuclei were observed at NMJs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: A pronounced decline in GFP-labeled SC-derived contribution in the vicinity of NMJs was observed in 18 and 24-month-old mice.
source: In accordance with the timing of SC loss during aging (Sousa-Victor et al., 2015) and a potential role for SCs in the lifelong maintenance of NMJs, we observed a pronounced decline in GFP-labeled SC-derived contribution in the vicinity of NMJs in 18 and 24-month-old mice (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by single myofiber analysis shown in Figure 3B–D, and citation to previous literature (Sousa-Victor et al., 2015).

claim: SC depletion markedly accelerated sarcopenia-related NMJ deterioration, with induction of degenerated NMJs at 12 months in P7DTA mice.
source: Examination of P7DTA NMJs revealed induction of degenerated NMJs at 12 months, indicating that SC depletion markedly accelerated sarcopenia-related NMJ deterioration (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by NMJ analysis data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: Prior to significant induction of partial innervation, a significant increase in the proportion of NMJs with 0–2 post-synaptic myonuclei was observed at 12 months compared to 6 month-old muscles.
source: Prior to significant induction of partial innervation, a significant increase in the proportion of NMJs with 0–2 post-synaptic myonuclei was observed at 12 months compared to 6 month-old muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The exacerbated deterioration of NMJs at 12 months, as a result of SC depletion, was associated with a further decline in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters.
source: Indeed, the exacerbated deterioration of NMJs at 12 months, as a result of SC depletion, was also associated with a further decline in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters (Figure 3F and I, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by NMJ analysis data shown in Figure 3F and I, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: A reduction in the proportion of fast type IIX myofibers with age was observed, but the onset or severity of this phenotype was not altered upon SC depletion.
source: Although we observed a reduction in the proportion of fast type IIX myofibers with age, the onset or severity of this phenotype was not altered upon SC depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by myofiber type composition analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: Significant reduction in cross-sectional area of myofibers was observed upon SC depletion at 12 months.
source: The examination of single myofibers isolated from EDLs, fixed prior to dissection, revealed significant reduction in cross-sectional area of myofibers upon SC depletion at 12 months (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by myofiber CSA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5C and D.

claim: SC depletion is sufficient to induce early onset of sarcopenia phenotypes, specifically NMJ deterioration and myofiber atrophy without evidence of gross denervation.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that SC depletion is sufficient to induce early onset of sarcopenia phenotypes, specifically NMJ deterioration and myofiber atrophy without evidence of gross denervation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on NMJ degeneration and myofiber atrophy in SC-depleted mice.

claim: The suppression of Spry1 has been linked to SC pool loss in aged muscles.
source: The suppression of Spry1, a downstream target and negative-feedback modulator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) /fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling (Kim and Bar-Sagi, 2004), has been linked to SC pool loss in aged muscles (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Bigot et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Kim and Bar-Sagi, 2004; Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Bigot et al., 2015).

claim: Forced expression of Spry1 in SCs attenuates age-associated SC decline.
source: Moreover, the forced expression of Spry1 in SCs attenuates age-associated SC decline (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Bigot et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Bigot et al., 2015).

claim: Aged muscles from Spry1OX mice with tamoxifen administered at 12 months had significantly more SCs.
source: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed that aged muscles from Spry1OX mice with tamoxifen administered at 12 months had significantly more SCs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and citation to previous literature (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).

claim: Age-related NMJ deterioration was attenuated in Spry1OX muscles, demonstrated by a reduction in the proportion of pre/post-synaptic degenerated NMJs.
source: Examination of NMJ integrity revealed that age-related NMJ deterioration was attenuated in Spry1OX muscles, demonstrated by a reduction in the proportion of pre/post-synaptic degenerated NMJs (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by NMJ analysis data shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: An increase in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters was observed in aged Spry1OX mice.
source: Also, an increase in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters was observed in aged Spry1OX mice (Figure 4B and E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B and E.

claim: Aged Spry1OX mice ran a significantly longer time/distance than Ctrl mice in treadmill exercise tests.
source: Aged Spry1OX mice ran a significantly longer time/distance than Ctrl mice (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by treadmill performance data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Significant increases were detected in peak absolute force generated by aged Spry1OX muscles in comparison to Ctrl muscles upon stimulation at frequencies of 100, 125 and 150 Hz.
source: Significant increases were detected in peak absolute force generated by aged Spry1OX muscles in comparison to Ctrl muscles upon stimulation at frequencies of 100, 125 and 150 Hz (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo force generation data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: No significant difference was observed in specific force (force normalized to physiological cross-sectional area) between aged Spry1OX and Ctrl muscles.
source: However, no significant difference was observed when force was normalized to physiological cross-sectional area (specific force), which accounts for modifications in muscle girth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by specific force data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Increased EDL myofiber cross-sectional area was observed in aged Spry1OX mice without significant changes in myofiber type composition or number.
source: Indeed, we observed increased EDL myofiber cross-sectional area without significant changes in myofiber type composition or number in aged Spry1OX mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by myofiber analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: Preventing age-related SC loss through stimulation of Spry1 expression in SCs was associated with the prevention of post-synaptic myonuclear loss, myofiber atrophy, and force generation capacity decline in aged skeletal muscles.
source: Therefore, preventing age-related SC loss, through stimulation of Spry1 expression in SCs without direct peripheral nerve manipulation, was associated with the prevention of post-synaptic myonuclear loss, myofiber atrophy, and force generation capacity decline in aged skeletal muscles.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on SC preservation, NMJ integrity, myofiber size, and force generation in Spry1OX mice.

claim: Loss of SC contribution drives age-related NMJ degeneration.
source: In this report, we find marginal denervation in aged skeletal muscles, and that loss of SC contribution drives age-related NMJ degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing SC depletion accelerates NMJ degeneration and SC preservation attenuates it.

claim: SCs are a source of post-synaptic myonuclei.
source: Specifically, SCs are a source of post-synaptic myonuclei.
evidence: Supported by fate tracking experiments showing GFP-labeled post-synaptic myonuclei derived from SCs.

claim: With age, SC-derived contribution of myonuclei to the post-synaptic region is compromised, which links to age-related NMJ degeneration.
source: With age SC-derived contribution of myonuclei to the post-synaptic region is compromised, which accordingly links to age-related NMJ degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing reduced SC-derived contribution at NMJs in aged mice and correlation with NMJ degeneration.

claim: Denervation is likely not a principal mechanism driving age-related NMJ degeneration.
source: In aged skeletal muscles we did not observe characteristics of robust denervation, therefore denervation is likely not a principal mechanism driving age-related NMJ degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of denervation markers in aged muscles.

claim: Myonuclei clustered beneath the post-synaptic membrane of the NMJ within the myofiber are transcriptionally distinct from adjacent myonuclei and specialized for the expression of genes critical for NMJ function.
source: Myonuclei clustered beneath the post-synaptic membrane of the NMJ within the myofiber are transcriptionally distinct from adjacent myonuclei and specialized for the expression of genes critical for NMJ function (Chakkalakal and Jasmin, 2003; Schaeffer et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Chakkalakal and Jasmin, 2003; Schaeffer et al., 2001).

claim: Reduction in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters is associated with impaired NMJ development, ineffective regeneration after nerve insult, and neuromuscular diseases.
source: Reduction in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters is associated with impaired NMJ development, ineffective regeneration after nerve insult, and neuromuscular diseases (Liu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2007; Méjat et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Liu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2007; Méjat et al., 2009).

claim: Adult skeletal muscle possesses a remarkable capacity for regeneration endowed by a population of adult resident stem cells, satellite cells (SCs).
source: It is well established that adult skeletal muscle possesses a remarkable capacity for regeneration endowed by a population of adult resident stem cells, satellite cells (SCs) (Relaix and Zammit, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Relaix and Zammit, 2012) and established scientific knowledge.

claim: SCs, identified by the expression of the paired box transcription factor Pax7, are deemed to be the principal source of myonuclei for myofiber regeneration and repair.
source: Through depletion studies, SCs, identified by the expression of the paired box transcription factor Pax7, are deemed to be the principal source of myonuclei for myofiber regeneration and repair (Liu et al., 2015; Relaix and Zammit, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Liu et al., 2015; Relaix and Zammit, 2012).

claim: SCs contribute to NMJ regeneration.
source: In our previous study, we examined SC fate during NMJ denervation and reinnervation, and found that SCs contribute to NMJ regeneration (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Liu et al., 2015).

claim: Contributions of SCs and derived progenitors to myofibers have been observed during sedentary aging.
source: Recently contributions of SCs and derived progenitors to myofibers have been observed during sedentary aging (Keefe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Keefe et al., 2015).

claim: SC number and function decline with age.
source: Extensive studies have shown that SC number and function decline with age; however, whether this loss is connected to age-associated NMJ degeneration is unknown (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Sousa-Victor et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Sousa-Victor et al., 2015).

claim: Neuromuscular junction degeneration is a prominent aspect of sarcopenia, the age-associated loss of skeletal muscle integrity.
source: Neuromuscular junction degeneration is a prominent aspect of sarcopenia, the age-associated loss of skeletal muscle integrity.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a known fact about sarcopenia.

claim: Muscle stem cells activate and contribute to mouse neuromuscular junction regeneration in response to denervation.
source: Previously, we showed that muscle stem cells activate and contribute to mouse neuromuscular junction regeneration in response to denervation (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Liu et al., 2015).

claim: Degenerated neuromuscular junctions in aged mouse muscles were associated with reduced contribution from muscle stem cells.
source: Here, we examined gene expression profiles and neuromuscular junction integrity in aged mouse muscles, and unexpectedly found limited denervation despite a high level of degenerated neuromuscular junctions. Instead, degenerated neuromuscular junctions were associated with reduced contribution from muscle stem cells.
evidence: Supported by the experimental findings described in the manuscript.

claim: Muscle stem cell depletion was sufficient to induce neuromuscular junction degeneration at a younger age.
source: Indeed, muscle stem cell depletion was sufficient to induce neuromuscular junction degeneration at a younger age.
evidence: Supported by the P7DTA mouse experiments showing accelerated NMJ degeneration.

claim: Prevention of muscle stem cell and derived myonuclei loss was associated with attenuation of age-related neuromuscular junction degeneration, muscle atrophy, and the promotion of aged muscle force generation.
source: Conversely, prevention of muscle stem cell and derived myonuclei loss was associated with attenuation of age-related neuromuscular junction degeneration, muscle atrophy, and the promotion of aged muscle force generation.
evidence: Supported by the Spry1OX mouse experiments showing improved NMJ integrity and muscle function.

claim: Deficiencies in muscle stem cell fate and post-synaptic myogenesis provide a cellular basis for age-related neuromuscular junction degeneration and associated skeletal muscle decline.
source: Our observations demonstrate that deficiencies in muscle stem cell fate and post-synaptic myogenesis provide a cellular basis for age-related neuromuscular junction degeneration and associated skeletal muscle decline.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing the role of SCs in NMJ maintenance.

claim: Age-related neuromuscular junction declines in rodents and humans manifest as altered pre-synaptic nerve terminal and abnormal post-synaptic morphology indicative of degeneration.
source: Age-related neuromuscular junction (NMJ, synapse between motor neuron and skeletal muscle cells) declines in rodents and humans manifest as altered pre-synaptic nerve terminal and abnormal post-synaptic morphology indicative of degeneration (Gonzalez-Freire et al., 2014; Oda, 1984; Wokke et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Gonzalez-Freire et al., 2014; Oda, 1984; Wokke et al., 1990).

claim: Whether age-associated NMJ remodeling primarily reflects deterioration of target muscle cells or the peripheral nervous system is unknown.
source: Although these disruptions are often associated with skeletal muscle dysfunction and disease, whether age-associated NMJ remodeling primarily reflects deterioration of target muscle cells or the peripheral nervous system is unknown (Kang and Lichtman, 2013; Banker et al., 1983; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as an open question in the field, with citations to previous literature (Kang and Lichtman, 2013; Banker et al., 1983; Li et al., 2011).

claim: Spry1 is a downstream target and negative-feedback modulator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)/fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling.
source: The suppression of Spry1, a downstream target and negative-feedback modulator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) /fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling (Kim and Bar-Sagi, 2004), has been linked to SC pool loss in aged muscles (Chakkalakal et al., 2012; Bigot et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Kim and Bar-Sagi, 2004).

claim: Denervation stemming from sciatic nerve injury in adults or through genetic disruption of critical NMJ regulators in the embryo leads to robust elevation or induction of extra-synaptic expression of synapse-enriched genes.
source: Furthermore, denervation stemming from sciatic nerve injury in adults or through genetic disruption of critical NMJ regulators in the embryo leads to robust elevation or induction of extra-synaptic expression of synapse-enriched genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Liu et al., 2015; Sanes and Lichtman, 1999).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to previous literature (Liu et al., 2015; Sanes and Lichtman, 1999).

claim: Loss of NMJ-organizers such as Agrin or Laminin-α4 is sufficient to induce denervation.
source: Although loss of NMJ-organizers such as Agrin or Laminin-α4 is sufficient to induce denervation, these molecules are not lost with age (Samuel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Samuel et al., 2012).

claim: Agrin and Laminin-α4 are not lost with age.
source: Although loss of NMJ-organizers such as Agrin or Laminin-α4 is sufficient to induce denervation, these molecules are not lost with age (Samuel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Samuel et al., 2012).

claim: Insults in relatively close proximity to nerve terminals that lead to reinnervation, even in aged skeletal muscle, result in efficient repair without degenerated morphology.
source: In contrast, insults in relatively close proximity to nerve terminals that lead to reinnervation, even in aged skeletal muscle, result in efficient repair without degenerated morphology (Kang and Lichtman, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Kang and Lichtman, 2013).

claim: Sciatic nerve disruption-mediated denervation at a considerable distance from the target lower limbs and subsequent reinnervation leads to a high fraction of NMJs with degenerated morphology in adult mice.
source: For instance we previously demonstrated, in adult mice, sciatic nerve disruption-mediated denervation at a considerable distance from the target lower limbs and subsequent reinnervation leads to a high fraction of NMJs with degenerated morphology (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Liu et al., 2015).

claim: Denervation is sufficient to trigger extensive skeletal muscle atrophy and dysfunction.
source: Although denervation is sufficient to trigger extensive skeletal muscle atrophy and dysfunction, the proportion of completely denervated aged NMJs is modest (Figure 1B and D) (Liu et al., 2015; Oda, 1984; Wokke et al., 1990; Banker et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Liu et al., 2015; Oda, 1984; Wokke et al., 1990; Banker et al., 1983) and established knowledge.

claim: The proportion of completely denervated aged NMJs is modest.
source: Although denervation is sufficient to trigger extensive skeletal muscle atrophy and dysfunction, the proportion of completely denervated aged NMJs is modest (Figure 1B and D) (Liu et al., 2015; Oda, 1984; Wokke et al., 1990; Banker et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and D and citations to previous literature.

claim: Denervation with subsequent reinnervation can lead to degenerated NMJ morphology.
source: Denervation with subsequent reinnervation can lead to degenerated NMJ morphology.
evidence: Stated as a known phenomenon in the field.

claim: Laser ablation adjacent to endplate regions leads to local myofiber degeneration and regeneration with NMJ fragmentation.
source: Although laser ablation adjacent to endplate regions leads to local myofiber degeneration and regeneration with NMJ fragmentation, whether this insult affected the number, function, or recruitment of SCs or other skeletal muscle resident stem and progenitor cell types is unknown (Li and Thompson, 2011; Bentzinger et al., 2013; Judson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Li and Thompson, 2011; Bentzinger et al., 2013; Judson et al., 2013).

claim: Central nucleated myofibers, an indicator of degeneration and regeneration, have been observed in aged muscles.
source: Central nucleated myofibers, an indicator of degeneration and regeneration, have been observed in aged muscles (Valdez et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Valdez et al., 2010).

claim: Degenerative-regenerative events have been observed along the length of aging myofibers; however, such events leading to degenerated NMJ morphology in aged muscles are rare.
source: Moreover, degenerative-regenerative events have been observed along the length of aging myofibers; however, such events leading to degenerated NMJ morphology in aged muscles are rare (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Li et al., 2011).

claim: SC derived progenitor fusion into myofibers without appreciable central nucleation has been observed during aging, adolescent maturation, and denervation atrophy.
source: In contrast, we observed SC derived progenitor fusion into myofibers without appreciable central nucleation, consistent with previous reports during aging, adolescent maturation, and denervation atrophy (Liu et al., 2015; Keefe et al., 2015; Pawlikowski et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Liu et al., 2015; Keefe et al., 2015; Pawlikowski et al., 2015).

claim: During natural aging or upon SC depletion, loss of SC contribution is associated with NMJ degeneration.
source: During natural aging or upon SC depletion, loss of SC contribution is associated with NMJ degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing correlation between SC loss and NMJ degeneration.

claim: Post-synaptic myonuclear cluster size can be influenced by dissociation through the manipulation of proteins that anchor nuclei.
source: Post-synaptic myonuclear cluster size can be influenced by dissociation through the manipulation of proteins that anchor nuclei (Zhang et al., 2007; Grady et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Zhang et al., 2007; Grady et al., 2005).

claim: Aging is associated with loss of total number and normal spatial arrangement of myonuclei.
source: Aging is associated with loss of total number and normal spatial arrangement of myonuclei (Bruusgaard et al., 2006; Brack et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Bruusgaard et al., 2006; Brack et al., 2005).

claim: It is likely that both loss and dissociation contribute to reductions in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters with age.
source: Therefore, it is likely that both loss and dissociation contribute to reductions in the size of post-synaptic myonuclear clusters with age.
evidence: Inferred from the discussion of mechanisms affecting post-synaptic myonuclear cluster size.

claim: In primary cultures of aged human myoblasts, stimulation of Spry1 expression through global epigenetic modification promoted SC maintenance at the expense of myogenic differentiation.
source: In primary cultures of aged human myoblasts, stimulation of Spry1 expression through global epigenetic modification promoted SC maintenance at the expense of myogenic differentiation (Bigot et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Bigot et al., 2015).

claim: Forced expression of the related Spry2 during embryonic myogenesis favored retention of renewal competent as opposed to terminally committed myogenic cells.
source: Similarly, forced expression of the related Spry2 during embryonic myogenesis favored retention of renewal competent as opposed to terminally committed myogenic cells (Lagha et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Lagha et al., 2008).

claim: SC-specific Spry1 overexpression attenuates age-related SC decline without compromising myogenic differentiation.
source: In contrast, based on restoration of post-synaptic myonuclei, prevention of age-related atrophy, and improved force generation, we demonstrate that SC-specific Spry1 overexpression attenuates age-related SC decline without compromising myogenic differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the Spry1OX experimental results showing preserved SC numbers and improved muscle function.

claim: In the context of aging, Spry1 modifies FGF activity to regulate SC pool size at homeostasis.
source: In the context of aging, Spry1 modifies FGF activity to regulate SC pool size at homeostasis; however, the mechanisms of Spry1-mediated regulation of adult and aged post-synaptic myogenic differentiation are unknown (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).

claim: The mechanisms of Spry1-mediated regulation of adult and aged post-synaptic myogenic differentiation are unknown.
source: In the context of aging, Spry1 modifies FGF activity to regulate SC pool size at homeostasis; however, the mechanisms of Spry1-mediated regulation of adult and aged post-synaptic myogenic differentiation are unknown (Chakkalakal et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated as an open question in the field.

claim: Fusion of SC derived Spry1OX myogenic progenitors could lead to suppression of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) activity.
source: Furthermore, fusion of SC derived Spry1OX myogenic progenitors could lead to suppression of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) activity, which is elevated in skeletal muscle biopsies from chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) patients and sedentary aged individuals (Lemire et al., 2012; Williamson et al., 2003).
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism, with citations to previous literature (Lemire et al., 2012; Williamson et al., 2003).

claim: ERK activity is elevated in skeletal muscle biopsies from chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) patients and sedentary aged individuals.
source: Furthermore, fusion of SC derived Spry1OX myogenic progenitors could lead to suppression of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) activity, which is elevated in skeletal muscle biopsies from chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) patients and sedentary aged individuals (Lemire et al., 2012; Williamson et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Lemire et al., 2012; Williamson et al., 2003).

claim: In addition to maintaining skeletal muscle regenerative potential, Spry1 manipulation provides a viable approach for counteracting sarcopenia-related NMJ deterioration and aged muscle function decline.
source: Regardless, in addition to maintaining skeletal muscle regenerative potential, Spry1 manipulation provides a viable approach for counteracting sarcopenia-related NMJ deterioration and aged muscle function decline.
evidence: Inferred from the Spry1OX experimental results showing improved NMJ integrity and muscle function.

claim: Loss of myofiber regenerative potential endowed in SCs is a significant mediator of age-related NMJ degeneration.
source: Collectively, our observations, obtained through multiple lines of query, demonstrate that loss of myofiber regenerative potential endowed in SCs is a significant mediator of age-related NMJ degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing the role of SCs in NMJ maintenance.
